summary: Describes using AES with 192- and 256-bit keys in Secure RTP, including counter mode encryption for SRTP and SRTCP and a key derivation function. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Adds two stronger lock sizes to the system that scrambles audio and video calls.

questions: which srtp crypto suites use aes-192
what key derivation function goes with aes-256 in srtp
why use aes-256 instead of aes-128 for srtp
subtitle: How to use the larger 192-bit and 256-bit AES keys to encrypt secure audio and video streams.

tldr.problem: Secure RTP (SRTP) was defined around AES with a 128-bit key. Some users want a more conservative security margin, for example because the Suite B profile requires AES-256 for TOP SECRET information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the existing SRTP counter mode and key derivation function unchanged, only swapping in AES-192 or AES-256 as the block cipher. It then defines four crypto suites that bundle those ciphers with HMAC-SHA1 authentication.
tldr.outcome: SRTP gets AES_192_CM and AES_256_CM, matching key derivation functions, and four registered suites. It adds to the RFC 3711 functions and does not replace them.

today: RFC 6188 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 3711 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Why Larger AES Keys for SRTP
sections.content:
RFC 6188 describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with 192- and 256-bit keys inside Secure RTP (SRTP, defined in RFC 3711). It calls the ciphers AES-192 and AES-256, and AES with a 128-bit key AES-128.

The RFC admits that AES-128 is widely regarded as more than adequately secure. Some users still want a highly conservative strategy. For instance, the Suite B profile requires AES-256 for the protection of TOP SECRET information. The new crypto suites still use HMAC-SHA-1, which Suite B does not include.

The functions here are an addition to, and not a replacement for, the functions in RFC 3711.
sections.eli5: Most people are happy with a normal lock, but some want a bigger one just to be extra safe. This document adds the bigger locks.

sections.title: AES-192 and AES-256 Counter Mode Encryption
sections.content:
RFC 3711 already defines AES counter mode (called AES_CM), and that definition works for every AES key size. This RFC names the new variants AES_192_CM and AES_256_CM.

The only difference from AES_CM is the block cipher: AES_192_CM uses AES-192 and AES_256_CM uses AES-256. The inputs to the cipher are formed, and the outputs processed, exactly as in AES_CM. Both new ciphers take a 112-bit salt as input, as AES_CM does.

In counter mode a counter block is built from the salt, the SSRC from the RTP header, a packet index and a block counter that increases for each AES encrypt call. The result is a keystream block that is combined by exclusive-or with the data.
sections.eli5: The scrambling recipe stays exactly the same. Only the size of the secret key changes, from medium to big or extra big.

sections.title: The AES_192_CM_PRF and AES_256_CM_PRF Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
SRTP does not use its master key directly. It runs a key derivation function, also called a pseudo-random function (PRF), to produce the keys it needs. RFC 3711 defines the AES counter mode version, AES_CM PRF, which works with any AES key size.

This RFC names the new versions AES_192_CM_PRF and AES_256_CM_PRF. As with encryption, only the AES key size changes. The counter block carries an 8-bit constant label that differs for each kind of key being generated, together with the master salt and a block counter. Both new PRFs use a 112-bit salt.

The test vectors show three outputs per derivation: the cipher key, the cipher salt and the authentication key. The authentication key is 20 octets, so the last AES output block is truncated to 4 bytes.
sections.eli5: SRTP makes fresh working keys from one big master key, like cutting many copies of a key from one blank. The recipe stays the same and just uses the bigger AES.

sections.title: Which Key Derivation Function Goes with Which Cipher
sections.content:
The pairing rules use RFC 2119 words. When AES_192_CM encrypts, AES_192_CM_PRF SHOULD derive the keys and AES_128_CM_PRF MUST NOT. When AES_256_CM encrypts, AES_256_CM_PRF SHOULD be used, and neither AES_128_CM_PRF nor AES_192_CM_PRF is allowed.

A bigger PRF may serve a smaller cipher: AES_256_CM_PRF MAY be used with AES_CM and with AES_192_CM, and AES_192_CM_PRF MAY be used with AES_CM.

The rationale is that the cryptographic strength of key derivation must meet or exceed that of the encryption. Using the same function for both is natural but not required, so other key derivation functions can be defined later.
sections.eli5: The tool that makes the keys must be at least as strong as the lock it makes keys for, never weaker.

sections.title: The Four Crypto Suites
sections.content:
A crypto suite is a named bundle of parameters, described in Section 8.2 of RFC 3711. This RFC defines four, registered for use with SDP Security Descriptions (RFC 4568). Other SRTP key management methods are encouraged to reuse these definitions.

All four use HMAC-SHA1 for authentication with a 160-bit key, a 112-bit master salt and a default key lifetime of 2^31 packets. The suites differ in the master key length (192 or 256 bits) and in the SRTP authentication tag length (80 or 32 bits). The SRTCP tag is 80 bits in every suite.

Authentication keys stay at 160 bits on purpose. HMAC-SHA1 has only 160 bits of internal state, so larger keys would not improve resistance to attack, and keeping 160 bits maximizes compatibility with existing suites and implementations.
sections.eli5: A crypto suite is a ready-made kit of settings. There are four kits: two sizes of lock, each with a longer or a shorter tamper seal.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that AES-128 gives more than enough confidentiality today, since breaking it costs far more than theft, bribery or wiretapping. Larger keys are a fallback plan in case of unanticipated cryptanalytic results. AES-192 is regarded as secure even against some adversaries for which breaking AES-128 may be feasible, and AES-256 likewise relative to AES-192.

It is conjectured that AES-256 provides adequate security even against an adversary with a quantum computer working on 256 or more quantum bits. No such computer is known to exist.

The cost is a 40% increase in computational cost for AES-256 over AES-128. AES-256 SHOULD be used when the highest possible security is desired, and AES-192 MAY be used when more than AES-128 is wanted. The related-key attacks in the theoretical literature do not apply because keys come from a strong pseudo-random source.

Ideally the authentication key would also be 192 or 256 bits, but this is not security critical: a forgery attack against a session closes when that session closes. For this reason the RFC defines new ciphers but no new authentication functions.
sections.eli5: A bigger lock costs a bit more effort to turn each time, but it stays safe even if lock-pickers get cleverer in the future.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Section 7 gives test data based on Appendix B of RFC 3711 so implementers can check their work. It has keystream examples for AES-256 and AES-192 counter mode, covering a keystream segment length of 1044512 octets (65282 AES blocks).

It also walks through an initial key derivation for AES_256_CM_PRF and AES_192_CM_PRF. The master key is 32 octets for AES-256 and 24 octets for AES-192, each with a 14-octet master salt, and the key derivation rate is zero.
sections.eli5: The answer key at the back of a textbook: you run your own code and check that you get the same numbers.
